title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Introduction
content: A cystocele, otherwise known as a protrusion of the bladder, occurs when the bladder descends into the vagina. [1] The bladder bulges through the anterior wall of the vagina, with which it is anatomically associated. There are multiple underlying causes for the development of cystocele resulting in weakness of the muscles and the connective tissue surrounding the bladder and vagina.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Pelvic floor muscles and endopelvic fascia provide anatomical support for pelvic viscera in women. This pelvic support consists of 3 muscles: pubococcygeus, puborectalis, and iliococcygeus, which form a complex called the levator ani muscle group. In addition, the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments provide additional support and stabilization. A prolapsed or herniated bladder can hurt the quality of life, affecting daily functioning and sexual activity. In some women, symptoms may be mild and require no treatment, and, in some cases, prolapses regress following menopause. [2] On the other end of the spectrum, there are cases with slow progression of the condition, where the bladder can eventually completely herniate beyond the hymen.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Cystoceles result from a weakness of the pelvic-floor support system. The main associated risk factors are obesity, increasing age, and parity. They can also occur due to chronically increased intraabdominal pressure, collagen abnormality, family history of cystocele, and following pelvic surgery.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Obesity
content: Giri et al, in their systematic review, reported that women with a body mass index (BMI) greater than 25 had a risk ratio of 1.36 (95% confidence interval [CI]) for developing prolapse. In comparison, women with a BMI greater than 30 had a risk ratio of 1.47 (95% CI). [3] Another study suggested that in overweight and obese women, the risk of progression of a cystocele increased by 32% and 48%, respectively, compared with participants with normal BMI. [4] However, few studies have shown that weight loss did not lead to symptom resolution or regression of the prolapse. In particular, in some of them, weight loss was associated with a borderline worsening of uterine prolapse, indicating that the damage to the pelvic floor is irreversible. [5] [4]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Advancing Age
content: Several studies have shown a strong link between aging and vaginal prolapse. [6] [7] It is suggested that age-related changes in pelvic anatomy, innervation, and vasculature cause weakness in pelvic floor strength. [8] A study of vaginal tissue biopsies discovered that collagen in the vaginal wall changes its structure over time, which might explain the link between aging and cystocele development. [9]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Parity and Other Childbirth-related Factors
content: Vaginal delivery carries a high risk for pelvic floor weakness. [10] The attenuation of the pelvic floor muscles has been shown to increase with parity. Nygaard et al showed that the prevalence of pelvic floor disorders increases by 12.8%, 18.4%, 24,6%, and 32.4% for 0, 1, 2, and 3 deliveries, respectively. [11] Moreover, it was found that forceps delivery plays a critical role in levator ani muscle avulsion. [12] Mant et al specifically suggest that the first stage of labor is responsible for developing a vaginal prolapse. [13]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Increased Intraabdominal Pressure
content: Increased intraabdominal pressure seems to have a weak correlation with anterior vaginal prolapse. Several studies indicated a correlation between cystocele development and constipation, chronic cough, and obstructive pulmonary disease, which are all associated with chronically increased abdominal pressure. [14] [15] [16]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Collagen Abnormality
content: The predominant type of collagen found in the vaginal wall is type III, designed to be resistant to sudden pressure changes, which is essential in tissues that require elasticity. In women with vaginal prolapse, the amount of collagen III in the vaginal tissue was higher than in healthy women, possibly due to the underlying remodeling. [9] Women with congenital conditions affecting collagen production, such as Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, are predisposed to developing cystocele. [17] [18] Up to a third of women with Marfan and three-quarters of women with Ehlers-Danols have a history of vaginal wall prolapse. [17]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Family History
content: Even though there are no known specific genes responsible for the development of vaginal prolapse, a review of 16 studies has revealed that women with pelvic prolapse are highly likely to have a relative suffering from the same condition. [19]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Etiology -- Pelvic Surgery
content: Surgery of the pelvis, especially hysterectomy, causes damage to the endopelvic fascia and nerves. This, in turn, results in a greater risk of vaginal prolapse and herniation of the bladder. [20]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: It is challenging to accurately estimate the number of women affected by anterior vaginal wall prolapse. This derives from many of these patients having minimal or no symptoms and, therefore, never presenting to medical professionals. Secondly, many patients feel reluctant to seek medical advice because of social embarrassment. The Women's Health Initiative study estimated that the prevalence of bladder prolapse is 34.3% for women with a uterus and 32.9% for women who have undergone a hysterectomy. [6]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: A cross-sectional analysis of 1961 nonpregnant women above 20 years old revealed that 2.9% of the participants had a degree of pelvic organ prolapse. [11] Symptoms were found to be more severe in populations of women from lower socio-economic backgrounds. It has also been shown that approximately 11.1% of women require an operative procedure for prolapse management by the age of 80, with about a third of them needing a repeat procedure. [21]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Vaginal prolapse includes prolapse of the bladder (cystocele), bowel (rectocele), or uterus. Prolapse occurs when the levator ani structures are weakened, and the pelvic fascia becomes overstretched. There are 4 main support sites; damage to these areas leads to a descent of pelvic organs through the walls of the vagina. According to the anatomical site, cystoceles can be classified as apical, medial, and lateral. Apical defect: Localized in the upper segment of the vagina and is caused by a defect of the endopelvic fascia; contributes to the development of stress urinary incontinence (SUI) because of the interruption of the urethra-vesical junction [22] Medial defect: Caused by the separation of the pubocervical fascia from connective tissue around the cervix and damage to uterosacral ligaments; can present as a large cystocele Lateral defect: Results in vaginal wall separation from the arcus tendinous, causing a reduction of the lateral vaginal sulcus on 1 or both sides

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Complaints related to bladder prolapse may be divided into vaginal pressure, urinary symptoms, sexual dysfunction, and, rarely, defecatory symptoms. To aid in history taking, a set of questions called the Pelvic Floor Impact Questionnaire (PFIQ) can be used to assess pelvic prolapse-related symptoms. [23]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Women may complain of a feeling of pressure or sensation that something is bulging or about to come out of the vagina. Usually, this symptom develops when the prolapse is at the level of the hymen or beyond. With advanced stages of bladder prolapse, discharge, bleeding, or vaginal pain may be present.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Urinary symptoms may include stress incontinence (SUI) or symptoms such as frequency and urgency associated with an overactive bladder. [24] Patients may have trouble initiating urination, have a feeling of incomplete evacuation, and, in later stages, experience bladder outlet obstruction due to bending of the urethra. Some women may report a need to press on the anterior vaginal wall to void successfully. [25]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Sexual dysfunction may be due to physical, psychological, or partner-related factors. Prolapses can result in dyspareunia, urinary incontinence during intercourse, obstruction, and dryness. [26] It is reported that sexual dysfunction is associated with fear and embarrassment due to the possibility of urinary incontinence during intercourse. [27] Defecatory symptoms are rare but most commonly include constipation and incomplete emptying. These symptoms are more common with posterior and apical vaginal wall prolapses.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: A vaginal examination should be carried out with the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. A cystocele is diagnosed and staged using the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification System (POPQ), which provides an objective description tool and measures severity. [28] If the vaginal walls are seen beyond the vaginal opening, mucosal tissues should be inspected for ulcerations or other lesions. The examination should be repeated with the woman asked to strain or "bear down" and cough with attention made to any episodes of urinary incontinence or flatulence.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Subsequently, examination with a Sims speculum is performed to visualize the vaginal walls better. Simulated apical support may also be performed to establish whether a pessary may be of benefit. This is achieved by using forceps or a cotton swab and pressing the vaginal apex. To conclude, a bimanual examination excludes any other masses or pelvic pathology.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: The POPQ system, introduced in 1996, is the most objective and standard tool for evaluating the severity of anterior wall prolapse. This system consists of 4 stages and is recognized by The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Stage 0: No prolapse Stage 1: Most distal part of prolapse is -1 cm (above the level of the hymen) Stage 2: Most distal part of prolapse is greater than or equal to -1 cm but less than or equal to +1 cm (≤1 cm above or below the hymenal plane) Stage 3: Most outside portion of the prolapse greater than +1cm but less than + (total vaginal length -2) cm (beyond the hymen; protrudes no farther than 2 cm less than the total vaginal length) Stage 4: Complete eversion of the vagina; most distal portion of the prolapse greater than or equal to + (total vaginal length -2) cm. [29]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Three stages are used for patients after removal of the uterus and 4 if the uterus is present. The POPQ system uses 6 measuring points of the vagina (2 at the front, 2 at the bottom, and 2 at the apex) to create a map of the prolapse in the sagittal section. All the measurements are recorded in centimeters, with the level of the hymenal plane serving as a point of reference. Negative numbers express points above the hymen, and positive numbers are used for points below the hymen.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: The anterior wall in the POPQ system has 2 points. Point Aa is in the middle part of the anterior wall. It can have a value varying from -3 to +3 cm, depending on the severity of the prolapse. Point Ba is the distance between Aa and the apex of the vagina. Another important measurement made is total vaginal length (TVL), which is the length from the cervix (or posterior fornix) to the hymen. Staging classification is discussed in the staging section. [28]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Another frequently used system is the Baden-Walker Halfway Scoring System. The system's downside is a lack of clear demarcations; thus, this system is not as precise as POPQ and is not recommended by leading medical societies. It consists of 3 grades: 0: Normal position for each respective site 1: Descent halfway to the hymen 2: Descent to the hymen 3: Descent halfway past the hymen

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Apart from physical evaluation, imaging and other tests serve to identify issues associated with bladder function or for the further evaluation of the prolapse. For example, medical photography may be used to record changes in the prolapse, especially preoperatively. Perineal floor ultrasound scan is used to identify the evulsion of the perineal muscles from the symphysis pubis, which can increase the risk of cystocele development 3 to 4 times. [30] Other studies include urodynamics, such as a cystourethrogram, to further assess urinary complications. If signs and symptoms suggest a urinary tract infection, culture and microscopy of urine samples may be helpful to guide management.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment of cystocele is only suggested for women who report symptomatic anterior wall prolapse. [31] It has been established that it is not uncommon for a Stage 1 prolapse to regress. [32]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Broadly, management of the condition can be divided into expectant, conservative, and surgical. All the options should be offered to the patient and thoroughly discussed as part of a treatment plan. Better outcomes are noted if surgical objectives and the patient's expectations are discussed before treatment. [33]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Cystocele management requires careful consideration of several factors, such as a woman's age, physical and sexual activity, future reproductive wishes, the nature and extent of the symptoms, the degree of the prolapse, associated uterine or posterior wall prolapse, and incontinence symptoms. It also depends on surgical expertise & previous management outcomes.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Expectant Management
content: A "watch and wait" approach may be a good option for asymptomatic patients with low-grade cystoceles or for those who can tolerate mild symptoms. Some patients may not wish to have treatment for various reasons. In this case, high-grade cystoceles require frequent assessments of their symptoms to ensure no complications or changes in symptom burden.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Conservative Management
content: There are 2 main types of conservative management, vaginal pessaries and pelvic muscle exercises. The benefit of conservative management is that it does not impose operative risks, such as infection, bleeding, pain, a failed procedure, or anesthetic risk in a high-risk patient with comorbidities.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Conservative Management
content: Vaginal pessaries are the most popular conservative management option. Pessaries are plastic or silicone devices that are inserted into the apex of the vagina. They lift and support the vaginal walls, reducing the symptoms of pelvic organ prolapse. They are contraindicated with acute infection of the vagina or pelvis in those who have allergies to pessary materials and in non-compliant women.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Conservative Management
content: Kegel exercises (pelvic muscle exercises) can be advised for women with stage 1 or 2 prolapse. It is found that these exercises improve prolapses by 1-2 cm on average. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle therapy (PFMT) showed that women involved in pelvic muscle training showed better outcomes regarding symptoms and reduction of the size of the prolapse compared to control groups. [34] Supervised muscle training for at least 12-16 weeks can be considered for such women to measure the improvement. [35] The exercises should be continued if they are beneficial for the patient.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Conservative Management
content: Hormone replacement therapy is not a treatment for cystocele. There is no evidence that estrogen's topical or systemic use reduces the size of cystocele; the creams or estrogen-containing vaginal pessaries can still be used for women with cystocele for treating signs of vaginal atrophy, which may occur concurrently. [36] Another study has shown the pre-operative use of topical estrogen creams improves the synthesis of collagen, preventing thinning of the vaginal wall and reducing the activity of degrading enzymes. [37] It is essential to encourage the patient to work on modifiable risk factors, such as a high BMI (>30), smoking, heavy lifting, chronic cough, or constipation.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Surgical management is the next step for symptomatic women, those who require immediate relief, those who have declined conservative treatment, or for whom the conservative approach has failed to provide benefit. It should be noted that surgical management should follow the completion of the patient’s family as the pelvic support system can be further damaged during labor.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Surgical planning depends on whether the anterior vaginal prolapse is isolated or is combined with apical or posterior vaginal prolapse. A careful examination is required as a part of preoperative planning.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Anterior colporrhaphy
content: Anterior repair is performed trans-vaginally to repair central vaginal wall defects and to lessen the size of the anterior vaginal wall. For this procedure, a patient is placed in the lithotomy position and catheterized; a Sims speculum is inserted to better view the defect. An Allis forceps are placed at the midline of the anterior wall, 1 cm proximal to the urethra, and 2 more forceps on each side next to the cervix or the vaginal cuff. Local infiltration with an adrenaline/lidocaine solution is commonly used to achieve hydrodissection analgesia, and to minimize intraoperative bleeding. With the use of Metzenbaum scissors, dissection of vaginal mucosa from the underlying vesicovaginal fascia is performed. When the mucosal layer is entirely free, folding the muscular layer and adventitia using figure-of-eight sutures is performed. Careful placement of the sutures is crucial not to damage the bladder.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Anterior colporrhaphy
content: 2-0 Vicryl or PDS sutures are most often used. After successful plication, the excessive vaginal mucosa is removed, and the wound is closed with absorbable sutures. The surgeon should be careful not to reduce the diameter of the vagina too much, as later it may cause pain during sexual intercourse. One study reported that the success rate of surgical approaches ranged from 63% to 76.5%, depending on the procedure followed. [38]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Treatment / Management -- Sacral Colpopexy
content: The other way to repair a bladder prolapse is to perform a sacral colpopexy, usually done laparoscopically. This procedure aims to place a permanent mesh to the anterior and posterior walls of the vagina and then attach it to the anterior longitudinal ligament below the sacral promontory. The operation can be performed together with anterior colporrhaphy or on its own. The benefit of sacral colpopexy is that it avoids vaginal incisions and scarring, which results in a lower risk of vaginal shortening or dyspareunia. The success rate of this procedure is 60% to 89%. [39] A randomized trial indicated that laparoscopic sacral colpopexy has a higher success rate and a lower chance of repeat procedures for both anterior and posterior vaginal prolapses. [40] In many countries, including the US and the UK, the use of mesh for cystocele repairs has been suspended since 2019, pending an investigation into their use. [41]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Many different conditions could mimic the symptoms of bladder prolapse and should be included in the differential diagnosis, such as rectal or uterine prolapse, ovarian or uterine benign and malignant tumors, vulvar malignancy, or benign vulvar lesions such as Bartholin’s or Skene’s cyst, urethral diverticulum and other causes of incontinence, urinary retention or hyperreactive bladder.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: A cystocele is not a life-threatening condition on its own. However, it is progressive, and if left without proper management, it can cause a myriad of symptoms and conditions. Due to the protrusion of the bladder wall into the vagina, women might experience urinary symptoms and voiding dysfunction, which might be implicated with urinary tract infections and kidney damage. If the prolapse is beyond the vaginal opening, the mucosal tissue of the vagina can develop ulcers, and it is more prone to bleeding and infection. The psychological burden stemming from sexual dysfunction and urinary incontinence can also be significant.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Complications
content: Complications related to cystocele can be categorized depending on the type of management the patient receives. If a woman refuses or is noncompliant with treatment, the disease's natural course may lead to a complete vaginal prolapse (procidentia). Conservative management has its pitfalls. For example, vaginal pessaries can cause pain, erosion of the vagina, bleeding, or infection. [42]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Complications
content: Surgical procedures carry the most significant number of complications. The most common is the recurrence of the prolapse and a need for further repair. Around 40% of women require a repeat procedure after an anterior colporrhaphy due to symptom recurrence. [43] Other complications include postoperative bleeding, hematoma, damage to the surrounding pelvic organs, infection of the operative site and dehiscence of the wound, infection of the urinary tract, pain during intercourse, urinary retention, and the formation of a vesicovaginal fistula. There is also a higher rate of complications when using transvaginal mesh repair than using native tissue repair, predominantly in the form of chronic pelvic pain. [44]

content: The Association of Pelvic Organ Prolapse Support provides up-to-date information regarding vaginal prolapses, including anterior vaginal wall prolapse, and the POP (Pelvic Organ Prolapse) Risk Factor Questionnaire is also available on their website.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Due to the complex nature of anterior vaginal prolapse and its progressing effects on women's physical, mental, and sexual health, a multidisciplinary team's involvement is essential. Getting a broad group of specialists engaged in inpatient care provides support and significantly improves management outcomes.

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: According to the 2019 guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence, the multidisciplinary team for women with a vaginal prolapse should include a specialist-level doctor with experience in pelvic floor prolapse, an urogynecology specialist, an urogynecology nurse, and a pelvic floor specialist physiotherapist. [46]

title: Cystocele(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Additional members may include a member of the geriatric team, an occupational therapist, and a colorectal surgeon with an interest in pelvic floor surgery and expertise in operating in the obturator region in cases of concurrent rectoceles. For some cases, a radiologist with expertise in pelvic floor imaging, a pain team member, and a clinical psychologist might be required. [47] [48]
